question: Was Solomon alone when he sacrificed 1000 burnt offerings at Gibeon?
summary: 1 Kings 3:4 describes Solomon going to Gibeon and offering a thousand burnt offerings, with no mention of any congregation accompanying him. 2 Chronicles 1:3-6 describes the same sacrifice as a public event with "all the congregation" of Israel going up with Solomon to the high place at Gibeon.

reconcile.connective: Commentators read Kings' silence against Chronicles' fuller report, treating the sacrifice as one public national festival at which the king's nobles and the assembly were present as a matter of course.

discrepancy.connective: The objection is pressed by Steve Wells, compiler of the Skeptics Annotated Bible, who notes that Kings names no one but Solomon at Gibeon ('at least no one else is mentioned'), whereas Chronicles has 'all the congregation' go up with him.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptics Annotated Bible (1999; online at skepticsannotatedbible.com)

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament (1861-75), on 2 Chronicles 1:1-6
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: K&D treat this passage directly, arguing Kings and Chronicles are independent accounts of one event and that the Gibeon sacrifice was 'no mere private sacrifice' but a public consecration attended by the nation's representatives.

link.note: No allowlisted apologetics page treats this specific 1 Kings 3:4 vs 2 Chronicles 1:3-6 tension; the GotQuestions Solomon-high-place page does not compare the two accounts, so no link is cited.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The royal progress was of public importance. It was a season of national devotion. The king was accompanied by his principal nobility (Ch2 1:2); and, as the occasion was most probably one of the great annual festivals which lasted seven days, the rank of the offerer and the succession of daily oblations may help in part to account for the immense magnitude of the sacrifices.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly fills the gap: reads Kings' silent account as a public, attended event by importing Chronicles' 'principal nobility' (Ch2 1:2), so Solomon was not alone.
excerpts.source_note_text: the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there--The old tabernacle and the brazen altar which Moses had made in the wilderness were there (Ch1 16:39; Ch1 21:29; Ch2 1:3-6). The royal progress was of public importance. It was a season of national devotion.
